relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Israel's household is named through twelve sons.
The list completes the tribes without ranking their human worth.
Judah's household begins with a Canaanite mother and a remembered judgment against Er.
Tamar enters the line through Perez and Zerah, carrying survival into the royal genealogy.
Perez's line continues through Hezron and Hamul.
Zerah's descendants preserve names associated with wisdom and song.
Achar is remembered through a communal wound, but no descendant inherits his guilt.
Azariah carries Ethan's line.
Hezron's household branches into Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb.
Ram's line reaches Nahshon, a leader in Judah.
Nahshon leads toward Salma and Boaz.
Boaz leads toward Obed and Jesse.
Jesse's sons are counted from Eliab onward.
Nethanel and Raddai remain in the sibling archive.
David is named seventh, not as the only child who mattered.
Zeruiah and Abigail stand as sisters whose sons shape the later political story.
Amasa's parentage joins Abigail with an Ishmaelite father.
Caleb's household is remembered through Azubah, Jerioth, and their sons.
After Azubah's death, Ephrath enters the household and bears Hur.
Hur leads to Uri and the artisan Bezalel.
A daughter of Machir is married into Hezron's household and bears Segub.
Segub's son Jair becomes associated with many towns.
The genealogy remembers contested towns and shifting control across Geshur and Aram.
After Hezron's death, Abijah bears Ashhur, preserving a woman's labor beyond a man's life.
Jerahmeel's sons open another branch.
Atarah is named as wife and mother of Onam.
Ram's sons within Jerahmeel's house are remembered.
Onam, Shammai, Jada, Nadab, and Abishur continue the line.
Abihail is named as wife and mother.
Seled's death without children is recorded without making parenthood the measure of his worth.
The line continues through Appaim, Ishi, Sheshan, and Ahlai.
Jether's childlessness is recorded without erasing his place in the family.
Peleth and Zaza close this branch of Jerahmeel.
Sheshan's daughters and Jarha, an Egyptian servant, expose the archive's unequal household structures.
An unnamed daughter and Jarha become parents of Attai under power conditions the text does not explain.
Attai leads to Nathan and Zabad.
Zabad leads to Ephlal and Obed.
Obed leads to Jehu and Azariah.
Azariah leads to Helez and Eleasah.
Eleasah leads to Sismai and Shallum.
Shallum leads to Jekamiah and Elishama.
Caleb's branch connects Ziph, Mareshah, and Hebron.
Hebron's sons are remembered.
Shema and Rekem carry the line into towns and households.
Maon becomes associated with Beth-zur.
Ephah, a concubine, bears sons whose names survive while her unequal status remains visible.
Jahdai's descendants are named.
Maacah, another concubine, bears Sheber and Tirhanah.
Maacah's descendants are named, and Achsah appears as Caleb's daughter.
The line turns toward Hur, Ephrathah, and Kiriath-jearim.
Bethlehem and Beth-gader enter the family map.
Shobal's descendants and half of Menuhoth are remembered.
Families of Kiriath-jearim become communities rather than isolated male names.
Salma's line connects towns, households, and regional groups.
Scribal families at Jabez and Kenite-Rechabite ancestry close the chapter.

contemplative_note: This genealogy does not become holy by hiding its inequalities. It remembers Tamar's survival, unnamed daughters, foreign kin, concubines, artisans, scribes, and a servant incorporated into an elite household. Contemplative reading asks not only who is named, but who carried the line while someone else received the name.
